name: Guillain-Barre Syndrome

ethnicAssociations: Axonal variants (AMAN, AMSAN) more common in East Asia and Central/South America
AIDP most common variant in North America and Europe

criteria.description: Hyporeflexia or areflexia in weak limbs
Monophasic illness reaching nadir within 4 weeks (usually 2 weeks)
CSF albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein with normal cell count)
Electrodiagnostic features of demyelinating or axonal neuropathy
Preceding infection or triggering event 1-6 weeks before onset

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Progressive bilateral limb weakness plus hyporeflexia/areflexia. Supportive features include CSF findings and electrodiagnostics.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Variants include Miller Fisher syndrome (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia), AMAN (pure motor axonal), AMSAN (motor-sensory axonal), pharyngeal-cervical-brachial variant, and Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis.

pathognomonic.notes: Begins in legs, ascends to arms, then potentially bulbar and respiratory muscles
searchTerms: weakness starting in legs moving up
progressive limb weakness from bottom up

pathognomonic.notes: Diffuse loss of deep tendon reflexes

pathognomonic.symptomName: Rapid progression reaching nadir within 4 weeks
searchTerms: fast worsening reaching worst in 4 weeks
rapid decline to lowest strength within a month

common.notes: Nerve root pain; can be severe and precede weakness
searchTerms: aching in spine and arms or legs
muscle and joint pain in limbs and back

common.notes: Tachycardia, blood pressure fluctuations, urinary retention, ileus

laboratory: CSF albuminocytologic dissociation: elevated protein (>45 mg/dL) with normal WBC (<10 cells/uL)
CSF protein may be normal in first week
Anti-ganglioside antibodies: anti-GQ1b in Miller Fisher syndrome, anti-GM1 in AMAN
Preceding C. jejuni, CMV, EBV, or Zika virus serology may be positive
imaging: MRI spine may show nerve root enhancement with gadolinium
other: Nerve conduction studies: prolonged distal latencies, slowed conduction velocities, conduction block (AIDP) or reduced amplitudes (AMAN/AMSAN)
Serial forced vital capacity monitoring critical (<20 mL/kg suggests need for intubation)

distinguishingFeatures: CIDP progresses beyond 8 weeks; GBS peaks within 4 weeks
CIDP responds to corticosteroids; GBS does not
MG has fatigable weakness without areflexia
MG has normal nerve conduction studies
MG has decremental response on repetitive stimulation
Transverse myelitis has upper motor neuron signs
Spinal cord lesion on MRI in transverse myelitis

redFlags: Respiratory failure requiring intubation in ~25% of patients - monitor FVC and NIF serially
Autonomic instability can cause fatal cardiac arrhythmias
CSF pleocytosis (>50 cells) should prompt consideration of HIV, Lyme, CMV polyradiculitis, or leptomeningeal disease
Progression beyond 4 weeks suggests CIDP rather than GBS
Persistent areflexia without improvement after 4-6 weeks indicates poor prognosis
Bowel/bladder involvement early and prominently suggests spinal cord lesion rather than GBS
references: Shahrizaila N, et al. Guillain-Barre syndrome. Lancet. 2021;397(10280):1214-1228.
Willison HJ, et al. Guillain-Barre syndrome. Lancet. 2016;388(10045):717-727.
Fokke C, et al. Diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome and validation of Brighton criteria. Brain. 2014;137(Pt 1):33-43.
